title: The King Crowned with Thorns and Lifted Up
summary: Pilate has Jesus flogged and mocked, presents him to the crowd, and, pressed by the charge that releasing him would make Pilate no friend of Caesar, hands him over to be crucified. Jesus carries his cross to Golgotha, entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, and dies saying “It is finished.” A soldier pierces his side, and Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him in a new tomb in a garden.
story: Chapter 18 ended with the crowd choosing Barabbas. Now the trial before Pilate reaches its verdict and the hour Jesus has spoken of since Cana (2:4) arrives. Throughout the Gospel Jesus has said he would be lifted up and would draw all people to himself (12:32), and here the lifting up happens on a Roman cross. John tells the crucifixion with fewer details of agony than the other Gospels and more attention to meaning: Scripture fulfilled at each step, Jesus in control of his own death, and his kingship announced over the cross in three languages. The chapter ends in silence, with the body in a tomb as the Sabbath begins, and waits for the morning of chapter 20.
historical:
Crucifixion was Rome's most shameful form of execution, used chiefly for slaves, rebels, and those without citizenship. It was public by design, meant to terrorize. Victims were often flogged first with a whip of leather straps weighted with bone or metal, which alone could kill. The condemned carried the crossbeam to the place of execution, where he was tied or nailed to it and raised on an upright post. In 1968 an ossuary (a bone box) found at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem held the heel bone of a crucified man named Yehohanan with an iron nail still driven through it, the first physical evidence of crucifixion from the period. Death came slowly, often through exhaustion and suffocation, which is why breaking the legs hastened it.

The title fastened to the cross, the charge against the prisoner, was written in Hebrew (or Aramaic), Latin, and Greek, the languages of the land, of Roman law, and of the eastern empire. The site called Golgotha lay outside the city wall near a road. Since the fourth century, when the emperor Constantine built a church there, it has traditionally been located at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, which lay outside the walls in Jesus' day; the Garden Tomb, proposed in the nineteenth century, is a later alternative with less support from archaeologists. The crowd's claim that Pilate would be no friend of Caesar carried real weight: the emperor Tiberius was known for suspicion of disloyalty, and a governor accused of freeing a rival king risked his career.
cultural:
The soldiers' mockery parodies a royal investiture: a crown, a purple robe (purple dye was costly and associated with kings), and the greeting “Hail, King of the Jews!”, echoing the salute given to Caesar. Casting lots for the clothes was the executioners' perquisite. Jewish law required that the body of an executed man not remain on a tree overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22-23), and the concern was sharper because the next day was a Sabbath that coincided with the Passover festival, which John calls a High Sabbath.

Jewish burial did not embalm the body as the Egyptians did. The body was washed, wrapped in linen strips with spices to honor the dead and mask decay, and laid in a tomb, often a chamber cut into rock. The amount Nicodemus brings, about seventy-five pounds, is extraordinary, the kind of honor given at a royal burial. Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council according to the other Gospels, and Nicodemus, the Pharisee who first came to Jesus at night (3:1-2), both step into the open at the moment when association with Jesus is most costly.
literary: The chapter completes the trial scenes that began in 18:28, with Pilate going out and in, until at 19:13 he sits on the judgment seat. The Greek of that verse can even be read as Pilate seating Jesus on the judgment seat, and some interpreters think John intends that double meaning: the prisoner is the true judge. Two presentations, “Here is the man!” (19:5) and “Here is your King!” (19:14), frame the decision. At the cross John arranges five short scenes, each marked by fulfillment or testimony: the title, the garments, the mother and the disciple, the thirst and the last word, and the pierced side. He interrupts his narrative in verse 35 with an eyewitness claim, one of the clearest statements of purpose in the Gospel.

outline.t: Flogged, mocked, and presented: Here is the man
Pilate afraid: authority given from above
The judgment seat: We have no king but Caesar
Crucified at Golgotha under the title King of the Jews
Jesus gives his mother to the beloved disciple
I am thirsty; It is finished
The pierced side and the Scripture fulfilled
Burial by Joseph and Nicodemus in a new tomb

doctrines.note: Jesus dies on the day of Preparation, about the time the Passover lambs were being prepared, and John applies to him the Passover rule that none of the lamb's bones be broken (Exodus 12:46). John the Baptist's words at the start of the Gospel, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (1:29), come to their fulfillment here.

Pilate's title, written in three languages and refused revision, proclaims Jesus as King of the Jews. The chief priests' cry, “We have no king but Caesar,” is John's sharpest irony: in rejecting him, Israel's leaders disown the kingship of God himself.

Jesus tells Pilate his authority is given from above. Rome's power is real, but it is borrowed. The cross is at once the worst human injustice and the fulfillment of God's purpose, and John holds both without letting either cancel the other.

words.note: Teleo, to finish, complete, or fulfill. Jesus' last word in John is a single Greek word, tetelestai, “It is finished.” It is not a cry of defeat but of accomplishment: the work the Father gave him to do (17:4) is done. The same verb appears in verse 28, where Jesus knows that everything has now been accomplished. The word was also used for completing a task or paying off an obligation, though it should not be pressed into a technical term for a receipt.

Stauroo, to crucify. The verb rings through verses 6 to 23, first as the crowd's demand and then as the soldiers' act. In John's Gospel crucifixion is also the lifting up of the Son of Man (3:14; 12:32-33), so the most degrading form of death becomes the place where Jesus is exalted and his glory revealed.

Ekkenteo, to pierce. Used in the New Testament only here (19:37) and in Revelation 1:7, both drawing on Zechariah 12:10, where the people look on one they have pierced and mourn. John sees in the soldier's spear thrust the fulfillment of that prophecy of grief and cleansing.

christ: Everything in John has pointed here. Jesus is the King enthroned on a cross, the Lamb whose bones are not broken, the one who knows everything has been accomplished and gives up his spirit rather than having it taken (10:18). His concern for his mother in his last hour shows his humanity as clearly as his words show his authority. The flow of blood and water has been read in many ways: as proof that he truly died, as a sign of the life and cleansing that flow from his death (compare 7:38-39), and by many in the church as pointing to baptism and the Lord's Supper. John's stated purpose is simpler, that the eyewitness testifies “so that you also may believe.” The Son of God has truly died, which is the necessary ground of the resurrection that follows.

hard.q: Did Jesus die on the day of Passover or the day before, and why does John seem to differ from the other Gospels?
hard.a:
Matthew, Mark, and Luke present Jesus' last supper as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12), which would put the crucifixion on Passover day itself. John says the leaders had not yet eaten the Passover when they brought Jesus to Pilate (18:28) and that the crucifixion was on the day of Preparation for the Passover (19:14). John's timing also differs from Mark's third hour (Mark 15:25) for the crucifixion.

There are several responses. Some scholars conclude that John has shifted the timing to present Jesus as dying when the lambs were slaughtered, a theological rather than chronological choice. Others argue that the phrases can be harmonized: Preparation can mean the day before the Sabbath of Passover week (that is, Friday), and the Passover the leaders feared missing may refer to the festival meals later in the week. A third view holds that different groups followed different calendars that year. Ancient timekeeping was approximate, and the third and sixth hours were broad blocks of the morning. All four Gospels agree on the essentials: Jesus died on a Friday at Passover time, under Pilate, and rose on the first day of the week.

questions: Pilate says, “Here is the man!” What do you see when you look at Jesus crowned with thorns, and what does it tell you about the kind of king he is?
Joseph and Nicodemus had been secret disciples. Why do you think they came into the open at the moment of apparent defeat, and what would that cost you?
What do you think Jesus meant by “It is finished”? What difference would it make to live as if something truly has been finished for you?
